title: Is Privacy a Generational Question?
paragraphs: There is a story that every generation tells about the one that follows it: that the young no longer care about something the old hold sacred. At present, the story concerns privacy. Teenagers, we are told, post their lives online without a second thought, share their location with strangers and have no idea what they are giving away. It is an appealing story, partly because it flatters those who tell it, and I suspect it is largely wrong.

Consider what the young actually do. Researchers who have interviewed teenagers about their online habits often find a sophisticated understanding of privacy, though not always the one adults expect. Young people tend to manage who sees what with great care: they keep several accounts, use private groups, delete posts after a day and think hard about which friends might screenshot a message. This is not carelessness. It is a different, more flexible idea of privacy, in which control matters more than secrecy.

The older conception, which treats privacy as the right to keep information hidden, is easier to understand but harder to apply. In a world where almost everything is recorded, hiding has become nearly impossible. What remains possible is choosing the audience. A photograph sent to a close friend and the same photograph seen by an employer are, in a sense, different objects, even though the file is identical. Privacy, on this view, is about context rather than concealment.

Where the generations truly differ is in their experience of consequences. Adults who grew up before social media have seen how an old comment can resurface in a hiring decision or a political campaign, and they are rightly anxious. Many young people have yet to feel such consequences, and they cannot always imagine the person they will become. It is not that they care less; it is that they have had fewer opportunities to be hurt.

The real inequality, however, is not between old and young but between those who understand the systems and those who do not. Few users of any age read the terms and conditions of the applications they use, and fewer still know how companies combine small pieces of data to predict behaviour. A teenager who is careful about what her classmates see may still be unaware of what the platform itself knows. In that respect, we are all novices.

It follows that the solution cannot be to lecture the young. A more promising approach is to give everyone, of every age, better tools: clearer settings, honest explanations, and strong legal limits on what may be collected and sold. Such measures would protect the person who has never read a privacy policy as much as the one who has memorised it. They would also place responsibility where it belongs, with those who design the systems.

If there is a generational lesson, it may run in the opposite direction. The young have shown us that privacy is not a fixed object but a practice, something we do with attention and judgement every day. Those of us who learned the older idea might do well to learn the newer one, and, in turn, to lend the young some of the long memory that our own mistakes have given us.

title: The Strange Persistence of the Placebo
focus: Hedging, passive voice and cause-effect connectors
paragraphs: Imagine receiving a pill that contains nothing but sugar, and feeling better. This is the placebo effect, and it has been recognised for centuries, though only in recent decades has it been studied with serious tools. It is easy to treat the effect as a mere trick of the imagination, a polite way of saying that the patient was fooled. The evidence, however, suggests something more interesting: that expectation can change the body in measurable ways.

The effect is strongest where the outcome depends on perception, such as pain, nausea or fatigue. In studies of pain, volunteers who believe they have received a powerful painkiller report less discomfort, and brain scans show changes in the regions involved in processing pain. When researchers give a drug that blocks the body's natural opioids, part of the placebo relief disappears. This suggests that the brain, expecting help, may actually release its own pain-relieving chemicals.

What the placebo cannot do is equally important. It does not shrink tumours, cure infections or repair broken bones. Its influence is on how symptoms are felt and reported, not on the underlying disease. This distinction is sometimes forgotten by those who promote treatments of unproven value, who point to the patient's improvement as though it were proof of a cure. A patient may feel better and be no better, and honest medicine must be able to tell the two apart.

The most surprising findings concern honesty. In some small trials, patients with irritable bowel syndrome were told plainly that they were receiving placebo pills with no active ingredient, and that such pills had helped other people. Many still reported improvement compared with those who received no treatment. It appears that the ritual of care, the pill, the explanation and the attention of a clinician may be sufficient, even without deception. These studies were small, however, and larger trials are needed.

There is a darker twin of the placebo, known as the nocebo effect. Patients who are warned that a medicine may cause side effects are more likely to report them, even when the tablet is inert. Doctors therefore face an awkward dilemma: they must give patients full information, which is an ethical obligation, yet doing so can make unpleasant symptoms more likely. Some researchers suggest that the answer lies in how risks are presented, with emphasis on the proportion of patients who experience no problems at all.

The placebo also complicates the testing of new drugs. A medicine must outperform a placebo to be considered effective, and in some conditions, notably depression and chronic pain, the placebo response has grown stronger over time, making it harder to demonstrate an advantage. Reasons for this are debated; it may reflect changes in how trials are run or how patients are selected, rather than any real change in biology.

What should we conclude? Not that illness is imaginary, nor that care is a trick. If the doctor's manner, the clarity of an explanation and the confidence of a patient can affect recovery, then these things are part of treatment, not decorations around it. The placebo, far from being a nuisance to be eliminated, may be a clue to something that medicine ought to cultivate: the quiet power of being cared for.

title: The Potter of Ráquira
paragraphs: Before dawn, in a village in the Colombian highlands, Teresa Moncada is already at her wheel. Ráquira, in the department of Boyacá, has been known for its pottery for centuries, and its main street is a bright line of shops selling clay pots, little animals and painted bowls to visitors. Behind the shops, in a courtyard crowded with drying jars, Moncada is making something less colourful: a large, plain vessel for storing water, the kind her grandmother taught her to shape.

Moncada, sixty-three, learned the craft as a child, watching the women of her family. The method has barely changed. She digs the clay from a local hillside, removes the stones by hand, kneads it with her feet and shapes it without any machine except the wheel. 'People think that pottery is about being good with your hands,' she says. 'It is about being patient with the clay, because the clay decides how fast you go.'

The market has changed more than the method. When she was young, pots were sold for use; today, most are bought as souvenirs, and the shops prefer small, decorative pieces that fit in a suitcase. Large, practical vessels like hers earn a smaller income, and some neighbours have stopped making them altogether. A medium-sized water jar, which takes her a full morning, sells for about forty thousand pesos. A set of brightly painted miniatures, made in less than an hour, sells for almost the same.

Moncada does not resent the tourists. 'They come, they buy, they are friendly,' she says with a shrug. What bothers her is the pressure to imitate. A few years ago, a wholesaler offered to buy hundreds of pieces on condition that she copied a design popular in other regions. She declined. 'It would have paid the roof,' she says, 'but those pots would not be mine, and I would not recognise them.'

Instead, she has found other ways to sustain the work. Twice a week she runs a workshop for visitors, teaching small groups to shape a simple bowl. The sessions are short and noisy, and she enjoys them more than she expected. She also teaches a class at the village school, where several girls and two boys now come to the courtyard on Saturdays. 'If I do not teach them,' she says, 'the large jar will end with me.'

One of her pupils, a fifteen-year-old named Juliana, described the experience as unlike anything she had done at school. 'Nothing is done quickly. If you hurry, it collapses.' Juliana plans to study design in Tunja, but intends to return. Her mother, who works in a hotel, is lukewarm about the idea; pottery, she says, is not a career. Moncada, listening from the other side of the courtyard, pretends not to hear.

By mid-morning, the water jar is finished, and she sets it in the shade to dry. It will take a week to harden and another day in the kiln, and any crack will ruin it. She says there is no guarantee that the jar will survive, and the thought does not seem to trouble her. 'You make it as well as you can,' she says, wiping her hands on her apron. 'After that, it is between the pot and the fire.'

title: In Defence of Subtitles
paragraphs: A film is a strange object to translate. Unlike a novel, it does not consist of words alone; it is made of faces, voices, silences and music, all fused into a single experience. Any attempt to carry it into another language therefore requires a choice, and different countries have chosen differently. Spain, Italy, Germany and France have long preferred dubbing, replacing the original voices with local ones. The Netherlands, Portugal and the Nordic countries have chosen subtitles. Both choices have defenders, and I am firmly on one side.

The case for dubbing is not trivial. A dubbed film lets the viewer watch the screen without interruption, which matters for children, for people with reading difficulties and for anyone who simply wants to relax. A good dubbing actor can be remarkable, and in countries with a long tradition the craft reaches a very high standard. It would be unfair to dismiss it as a mere convenience.

Nevertheless, something is lost that cannot be recovered. A voice is part of the performance, as much as a gesture or a glance. When an actor pauses before a line, when her breath catches, when his accent reveals where he grew up, these details carry meaning. In a dubbed version, they are replaced by another performer's interpretation, however skilled. We are no longer watching one actor but the idea of a character voiced by two people.

Subtitles, by contrast, ask a little effort of the viewer, and give a great deal in return. They keep the original performance intact; they expose us to the sound of other languages; and they quietly teach us something about them. People who read subtitles regularly often pick up expressions, intonation and even vocabulary without trying. For language learners, this is a gift. A cinema that is always translated into one's own tongue shuts that door.

The usual objection is that reading is tiring and distracts from the image. In my experience, the discomfort fades remarkably quickly. After about twenty minutes, the eye learns to glance at the bottom of the screen and return without thinking, and many viewers report that they stop noticing the text altogether. As the director Bong Joon-ho observed when accepting an award in 2020, once you overcome the one-inch-tall barrier of subtitles, you will be introduced to many more amazing films.

There is also a matter of cultural confidence. A country that insists on hearing everything in its own language risks seeing the world only through that language. By contrast, a viewer accustomed to subtitles grows used to the idea that stories come from elsewhere and that they do not need to be domesticated in order to be enjoyed. This seems to me a healthy habit, particularly in an age of shrinking attention.

I do not wish to insist that everyone should prefer subtitles. Viewers should be free to choose, and platforms that offer both options deserve credit. But if I am asked which kind of experience is richer, I have no hesitation. A film is a performance by particular people in a particular tongue. To hear them is not a luxury; it is simply to watch the film that was made.

title: A Borrowed Voice
focus: Narrative past forms, inversion and reported speech
paragraphs: Valeria Ochoa had a voice that people trusted. It was low and unhurried, with a slight roughness at its edges, and for nine years it had announced the departures and arrivals at the central bus terminal of Quito. Passengers hurrying across the concourse slowed down when they heard it, as if the news of a delayed bus could not be so bad if she was the one giving it. Nobody knew her face. She preferred it that way.

On a Tuesday in March, the terminal's management announced that the announcements would be automated. A computer voice, trained on recordings of her own, would read the schedule from now on. 'It will sound exactly like you,' the manager said, in the tone of a man offering a gift. 'You will not need to come in.' He gave her six weeks' notice and a handshake that was a little too long.

She spent the first week furious. She walked through the terminal at lunchtime, listening to herself being replaced by herself in the test broadcasts. The imitation was good, which was the insulting part. It had her low register and even the rough edge, but it paused in the wrong places, as if the speaker had never been late for anything in her life.

On the Friday of the second week, an old woman approached her at the bus stop outside. She carried a basket of oranges and wore a hat pulled low over her eyes. 'You are the voice,' she said, not asking. 'I recognise you by the way you stand.' Valeria laughed, surprised that anyone could know her from her posture. 'Every morning I hear you say that the bus to Ambato is leaving,' the woman continued. 'It is how I know that the day has begun.'

Valeria did not tell her about the dismissal. She bought a kilo of oranges, paid five dollars, and let the woman keep the change, which was more than the woman had expected. As she walked back inside, she understood something that she had not been able to explain to the manager. It was not the sound that people trusted. It was the fact that, behind the sound, somebody was awake.

On her last day, she did something that was not permitted. Instead of reading the schedule, she added a sentence at the end of the final announcement. 'Good morning to those of you who are travelling, and to those who are waiting. Take care of one another on the road.' A pause followed, a real one, such as a machine would not have chosen. Then she switched off the microphone and went home.

The computer voice has been reading the schedule for three months now. It never makes mistakes. Yet the woman with the oranges still sits at the stop outside, and when she hears the announcement, she is said to look up for a moment, tilt her head, and sigh, as one does on realising that a familiar light has stopped coming from a window.

title: Urban Heat Island Study: Summary
focus: Formal report language and data description
paragraphs: ## 1. Background and method

This summary reports the main findings of a study of temperature differences within a large Argentine city. Between December and February, temperature sensors were installed at sixty locations, ranging from dense commercial districts to parks and residential neighbourhoods on the periphery. Readings were taken every ten minutes, and the results were compared with those from a reference station located outside the urban area. The study was commissioned by the city's environment department.
## 2. Principal findings

Throughout the study period, the city centre was consistently warmer than its surroundings, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. The difference was greatest at night, when central districts remained on average four degrees Celsius warmer than the reference station. During the hottest week, the gap exceeded six degrees in some locations.

Within the city, temperature varied markedly according to land cover. Locations with extensive tree cover recorded daytime temperatures three to five degrees lower than those surrounded by asphalt and concrete. Parks with mature trees were the coolest sites measured, whereas a large car park in the western district was the hottest, exceeding the average by more than seven degrees at midday.

The cooling effect of vegetation was not confined to the immediate vicinity of trees. Sensors placed two hundred metres downwind of the largest park recorded temperatures nearly one degree lower than those at comparable sites with no green space nearby. This suggests that moderately sized green areas can benefit surrounding streets, although the effect depends on wind direction and building height, factors that were not controlled in the present study.
## 3. Social distribution of risk

When the temperature data were overlaid with census information, a clear pattern emerged. The hottest neighbourhoods tended to be those with lower average incomes, fewer trees and a higher proportion of residents over seventy or under five. Households in these areas were also less likely to have air conditioning. In practical terms, those most vulnerable to heat were also those most exposed to it.

Hospital admissions for heat-related conditions during the study period were examined for a subset of the districts. Admissions were highest on days when night-time temperatures failed to fall below twenty-five degrees, which supports the view that the absence of overnight relief, rather than daytime peaks alone, is the factor most closely associated with health risk. Further research would be needed to confirm a causal relationship.
## 4. Recommendations

The study recommends that the city prioritise tree planting in the five hottest neighbourhoods, and that new developments be required to include shade and permeable surfaces. It further recommends that light-coloured materials be considered for roofs and roads, and that heat warnings be communicated directly to households in the most affected districts.
## 5. Limitations

Readings covered a single summer, and it would be inappropriate to generalise from them to other years. Sensors were not distributed evenly across all districts, and several experienced technical faults. Conclusions about causes should therefore be regarded as provisional. The authors recommend that the study be repeated for at least three summers before any large capital investments are decided.

title: Who Is Buying the Beach?
focus: Reporting verbs, passive voice and contrast
paragraphs: On a stretch of Costa Rica's Pacific coast, a fisherman named Esteban Araya recently arrived at the path he has used since childhood to find it blocked by a metal gate. A guard, polite but firm, told him that the beach beyond belonged to a private development and that access was restricted to residents. Araya said that he had never heard of such a thing. 'This was always the way to the water,' he told us. 'Nobody ever asked me for papers.'

Costa Rican law is, on paper, generous to the public. The first fifty metres of land from the high-tide line are public and cannot be owned or enclosed. The next hundred and fifty metres form a restricted zone, in which land may be leased by the municipality under a concession, but never sold. These rules, intended to guarantee that anyone can reach the sea, are among the strongest in the region. Their application, however, is another matter.

Our investigation examined the concessions in one coastal municipality over ten years. Of the forty-one that we could identify in municipal records, nineteen were held by companies whose registered addresses were abroad or whose shareholders could not be determined. Eleven had been transferred to new holders without any public announcement. In six cases, structures stood within the fifty-metre public strip, which the law does not allow.

Officials of the municipality acknowledged that monitoring is weak. 'We have one inspector for the whole coast,' said one, who asked not to be named. 'He covers more than sixty kilometres, and he does not own a car.' The mayor's office said that it intended to hire two more inspectors, and that all irregularities would be reviewed. It did not say when. Residents who have complained say that they have received no reply.

The developers, for their part, deny wrongdoing. The company behind the gated project told us that its permits were issued legally and that the gate was a security measure for residents, not an attempt to restrict public access. It added that fishermen were welcome 'with prior arrangement'. This phrase deserves attention, because the law says nothing about arrangements: the strip is public by right, and nobody is required to ask.

The consequences extend beyond access. Local fishermen say that when beaches are enclosed, they lose the landing places where they have traditionally launched their boats, and they are forced to travel further. Small restaurants that depend on beach visitors have noticed a decline in customers. A tourism operator, who is not opposed to development, said that the rapid enclosure of the coast 'kills the very thing visitors come to see'.

Lawyers who specialise in coastal law say that the fix is not complicated. Concessions should be published, inspections should be regular, and any building within the public strip should be reviewed and, if unlawful, removed. None of that requires new legislation. It requires money, attention and a willingness to apply the rules to people who can afford lawyers. Until then, Araya said, he will keep walking the old path, gate or no gate, and he intends to bring a few friends.

questions.q: Under Costa Rican law, the first fifty metres from the high-tide line can be owned privately.

title: The Group Project Is a Lie
paragraphs: Every student knows the ritual. A teacher announces a group project, and four people who barely know one another are assigned the task of producing a presentation in two weeks. Within days, the pattern forms. One person does most of the work, one does a little, one disappears until the night before and one contributes a font. On the day of the presentation, all four stand at the front of the class, and all four receive the same mark.

The justification, I am told, is that teamwork is a vital skill, and that students must learn to collaborate. I agree with the second half of that sentence. Where I disagree is the assumption that the group project teaches it. What it often teaches instead is that the conscientious person will do whatever is necessary, that the idle will be carried and that fairness is somebody else's problem.

Consider the position of the diligent student, who will usually be the one to organise the others. She sends reminders that go unanswered, rewrites other people's paragraphs at midnight and finally submits the work under four names, since the alternative is a poor mark for herself. This is not an experience of collaboration; it is a lesson in resentment. Many people who later describe themselves as hating teamwork acquired the feeling in precisely this way.

The free rider, for his part, is not always a villain. Some students are overloaded by jobs and family duties; others are shy, or genuinely unsure how to begin. A system that assigns identical marks to everyone offers little help to them either. It conceals their difficulties behind the group's average, and spares them the feedback that might have shown them what to do differently.

What would a better design look like? Firstly, clear roles, written down at the outset, so that nobody can claim that they did not know what they were supposed to do. Secondly, short individual reflections, in which each member explains what they contributed and what they learned. Thirdly, assessment of the process as well as the product: checkpoints at which the teacher sees how the group is working, rather than only the final presentation.

None of this is revolutionary, and a number of teachers I have met already do it. One of them, a lecturer in Rosario, asks her groups to keep a shared log, in which every meeting and decision is recorded. When trouble arises, she can see exactly where it began. Her students, she says, complain at first about the paperwork, and then admit that the log made the arguments shorter and fairer.

Teamwork is real, valuable and difficult. That is exactly why it deserves to be taught properly, and not merely to be assumed. Throwing four students into a room and hoping for harmony is like throwing four people into a swimming pool and calling it a swimming lesson. A few of them may learn to swim; the rest will learn to dislike water.

title: Reading the Rings: What Trees Remember
focus: Passive voice and complex noun phrases
paragraphs: Cut a tree trunk across, and you will see a pattern of concentric rings. Most people know that each ring represents one year of growth, but fewer realise how much information is stored in them. In a warm, wet year, a tree grows quickly and forms a wide ring; in a dry or cold year, it grows slowly and forms a narrow one. Over decades, these differences form a record, a kind of diary written in wood.

The science of reading such records is called dendrochronology. Its principle is simple, though its application demands care. Because trees in the same region experience the same weather, their patterns of wide and narrow rings tend to match. By overlapping the patterns from living trees, old timber from buildings and preserved wood from earlier centuries, researchers can build a continuous sequence stretching back thousands of years.

This sequence has several uses. The first is dating. If a beam in an old house shows a certain pattern, matching it against the reference sequence can reveal the year in which the tree was felled, sometimes to the exact season. Archaeologists have used the method to date wooden structures, ships and even musical instruments. A violin, it has been shown, can sometimes be dated by the tree from which its top was made.

The second use is reconstructing past climates. Because ring width responds to temperature and rainfall, a long sequence can reveal droughts, cold spells and volcanic eruptions long before instruments were invented. A few of the world's oldest living trees, such as certain bristlecone pines in North America, have been alive for nearly five thousand years, and their rings are a valuable archive. In Chile and Argentina, long-lived cypress trees have provided records for the Southern Hemisphere.

The method has limits. Trees respond to many factors, not just climate, including insects, fire, competition with neighbours and the local soil. A narrow ring may mean drought, but it may also mean that the tree was shaded by a taller one. Scientists therefore sample many trees from many sites, and they compare the results with other evidence before drawing conclusions. Even so, interpretations are sometimes revised.

In recent decades, tree rings have taken on a new importance. They allow scientists to place today's warming in a long perspective, by showing how past temperatures varied before human activity became a major influence. They also help to test climate models: if a model cannot reproduce a drought that tree rings record, something in the model may need adjusting. Such checks are among the quiet ways in which very old wood contributes to very modern debates.

There is something humbling in all this. A tree has no mind, yet it keeps accounts, faithfully noting each good year and each bad one. Standing beside a trunk cut across, one can touch a decade when a river flooded or a century when the rain failed. It does not tell us what to do. It simply reminds us, ring by ring, that the climate has always changed, and that we have never before been the ones changing it.

Tree-ring dating can be applied to wooden objects
Violins are made only from ancient trees

Overconfident about the results
Honest and balanced

To suggest that trees can count money
To give a vivid image of how it records good and bad years

A history of the invention of the saw

very short
without gaps
